primary.thesis: The state visit goes ahead on schedule. A White House state visit gives many filmed chances for a handshake: the South Lawn arrival ceremony, the Oval Office pool spray, the bilateral meeting, the joint press appearance, the state dinner and the departure. The market settles on the LONGEST of these, so it takes the maximum over several handshakes, not the typical one. Trump habitually holds a grip and pumps it for the cameras, especially in seated or side-by-side Oval Office photo ops. Xi keeps his handshakes restrained and formal, which caps the grip, because a held grip needs both men. A single Trump-Xi handshake usually lasts a few seconds. Taking the maximum over several filmed ones pushes the result into the 6–15 second range, while Xi's reserve makes a 15-second-plus grip less likely. Heavy press-pool and state-media coverage makes 'No Handshake' and 'Photographed only' very unlikely, provided Xi arrives.

basket.reason: Several filmed handshakes, including an extended photo-op grip, make a longest handshake of 6–10 seconds the modal outcome.
Trump prolongs grips for photographers, often turning to the cameras while still holding on. In the Oval Office or at the arrival ceremony that can plausibly stretch past 10 seconds.
With many filmed opportunities over a multi-day visit, it is unlikely that every handshake stays under 6 seconds.

failure_narrative: There are three ways the basket loses. (a) The visit is postponed or cancelled before October 7: a flare-up over tariffs, export controls, rare earths, Taiwan arms sales or a military incident derails it, and the market resolves 'No Handshake'. (b) The visit happens but relations are frosty. Xi keeps every greeting to a brief, formal shake, protocol limits the photo ops, and the longest filmed handshake comes in under 6 seconds. (c) Trump performs one of his marathon grips, for example holding on through a lengthy Oval Office photo spray, and the longest handshake goes past 15 seconds. Outcomes (a) and (b) are linked: both come from a deterioration in US-China relations in the days around the summit.
hedge_thesis: In the worlds where the primary fails through cancellation or a cold, clipped handshake, the US-China trade and security relationship has turned worse. Washington raises or threatens tariffs, or tightens chip export controls. Beijing answers with rare-earth export restrictions, halts US soybean and agricultural purchases, or lets the yuan weaken, and Taiwan-related tensions rise. The mechanism: a summit is only cancelled, or reduced to a minimal protocol greeting, when a substantive dispute has broken out. That same dispute appears as tariff announcements, commodity-flow retaliation and pressure on China-exposed chip stocks. So instruments that pay on US-China escalation should tend to pay in the worlds where the handshake basket loses.
